The incumbent will provide strategic leadership for programme planning, as reflected in the CREWS Operational Procedures, implementation oversight, monitoring and evaluation, results-based management, performance reporting, and organizational learning to ensure the effective delivery of development and institutional outcomes.

### CREWS Strategy

**Structural adjustment → reduced public budgets → deterioration of observation networks → poorer services → low political visibility → dependence on donor projects → capital investment without sufficient O&M (operation & maintenance) → further deterioration.**  

And this matters particularly for **agriculture**. A functioning NMHS (National Meteorological and Hydrological Service) is the national layer connecting global weather models and satellites to local rainfall, evapotranspiration, soil moisture, crop calendars, drought indicators and agricultural advisories. Without that layer, Africa can have access to some of the world's best global climate datasets while still having relatively poor operational weather and climate services locally.  

The economic case is actually quite strong: World Bank estimates have put the benefit-cost ratio of hydrometeorological investment in Africa at roughly 7:1. The problem has historically been less “does meteorology create value?” and more “who captures the value, and who has to pay the recurring bill?”  

CREWS says that its overall success is measured in terms of wider socioeconomic benefits, particularly:  

-   reduction in lives lost to extreme climate events;
-   reduction in livelihoods lost or affected;
-   number of people living in areas covered by early-warning services;
-   people's access to and receipt of those warnings.

So there is a deliberate distinction between capacity/output indicators and impact indicators.  

CREWS is explicitly aligning its MEAL framework with the UN/WMO-led **Early Warnings for All (EW4All)**. The CREWS Steering Committee specifically instructed the Secretariat to align its Theory of Change and MEAL framework with the emerging EW4All M&E framework and the **Early Warnings Maturity Index**.  

That means CREWS is becoming part of a broader architecture:  

-   Sendai Framework →
-   Paris Agreement / SDGs →
-   EW4All →
-   CREWS + SOFF + other financing mechanisms →
-   National EWS/NMHS investments


### EW4All Early Warnings Maturity Index

How mature is a country's national early-warning system, and where are its biggest capability gaps?  

| Dimension | What it asks |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **1. Disaster risk knowledge** | Does the country understand where hazards, exposure and vulnerability are? |
| **2. Detection, observation, monitoring & forecasting** | Can it observe hazards and produce reliable forecasts? |
| **3. Warning dissemination & communication** | Can warnings reach the right people, through appropriate channels, in a usable form? |
| **4. Preparedness & response** | Do authorities and communities know what to do when a warning arrives? |
| **5. Enabling environment** | Are governance, legislation, institutions, financing, technology, coordination and human resources adequate? |

| **ERA5-Land** | ECMWF / Copernicus C3S | Land-surface model driven by ERA5 atmospheric forcing | **~9 km (0.1°)** | 1950–present | Global land-surface reanalysis: precipitation, temperature, soil moisture, PET/ET, runoff, etc. |

### Purpose of the Assignment

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), through the **Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems (CREWS)** Accelerated Support Window (ASW), seeks to engage a Climate Modelling and Downscaling Expert. The consultant will work closely with **Meteo Rwanda** to generate and evaluate high-resolution climate projections while strengthening national technical capacity to independently undertake climate modelling, downscaling, validation, analysis and interpretation.  

Strengthen the technical and institutional capacity of Meteo Rwanda to generate, evaluate, interpret and apply high-resolution climate projections for Rwanda.  
The consultant will develop and apply an appropriate climate-downscaling methodology, evaluate available climate-model products against observations, generate and validate high-resolution projections of key climate variables and extremes, and strengthen the capacity of Meteo Rwanda staff to independently undertake and sustain these processes.  
The assignment will also support the development of climate information products that can be applied to early warning, climate-risk management, adaptation planning and climate-sensitive sectoral decision-making.

# Interview Thoughts


<a id="org274a729"></a>

## 3-year break

To lauch insurance product and operations in Ghana, but also in multiple food insecure countries at the same time was a major effort and changed my outlook on life’s priorities. Not being able to scale fast enough to retain venture funds, even though we signed MoUs with Togo and Ghana was distressing, almost tragic, because communities were deeply impacted. Yes in Ghana the public sector progressively enacted it’s own relief system through GAIC, leveraging some of our lessons learned, but there was no chance to really hand over the (local) teams and tech platform. Because we iterated so fast between seaons, it took me a while to personnaly digest and assimilate what we’d learned along the way, esp. where we made mistakes.  
In addition I came back from working with remote rural communities with parasitic infections that took a while to diagnose and that slowed me down for a good year.  


<a id="org363d02a"></a>

## Why Cyprus?

I was very inspired with 2021 PwC 15-year strategic plan for Cyprus (Vision 2035 for sustainable growth), was very high quality and inspiring work and demonstrated real engagement from the public sector.  

That study was paid for by ****EU DG Reform****.  

I’ve dedicated my whole life to equitable and sustainable development. Today in the Western world all these principles are put into question. Citizens’ well-being is no longer a priority and a guiding principle for today’s governments, so I prefer to move my focus elsewhere, where good public policy-making is still a local priority.  

In the past 2 years I took a break from my normal prodessional networks and interacted with musicians and artists.  

> This means that the growth model has Europe’s business and trade hub at its core, but is enhanced by the green and blue economy and the development of niche high-tech services (including in the research heavy areas of e-health, agritech and green technologies including renewables) to drive sustainability and diversification. By any means, this does not mean that we are favouring one sector over the other. All the sectors of the Cyprus economy have their role to play to deliver Vision 2035  


<a id="org394a444"></a>

## Agri-meteo, risks, preparedness, mitigation &ndash; 2026 where do we stand?

The upside of taking a sabbatical was that I was able to travel to new regions, esp. Russia, where I have contacts working for МЧС. To me that was a real eye-opener, because that Ministry focuses so much more on skill building for local populations and preparedness than what we’re used to in the West. Of course the focus there is no longer on food insecurity, but preparing for planting and harvest in the best possible conditions. I came back with the strong belief that good public policy means developing local information networks, decision-making systems, recommandations, skills, and logistics before disasters strike (not just early warning and insurance).  

2-week weather forecast were even more useful to farmers than automated insurance payments, because that give them sufficient lead time to adjust planting strategies and labor use. Esp. in terms of choosing specific crop varieties (short or long maturation), types of inputs, etc.  

Basically these are services you’d expect from ****top-notch agricultural and agro-meteo extension systems****, which no longer exist in Africa for lack of public funding (also underfunded in the West).

## MEAL


### How to design a MEAL plan that donors actually trust?

Ref: <https://lnkd.in/p/eAN3zXT9>  

After 15 years managing MEAL across USAID, EC, FCDO, and UN-funded programmes, here is what separates a MEAL plan that earns confidence from one that satisfies a submission requirement and nothing more.  

-   Start with the questions, not the indicators

    A MEAL plan built around indicators is a reporting tool. A MEAL plan built around evaluation questions what do we need to know, by when, and why is a learning tool. Donors increasingly know the difference. Start with: what are the three most important things we need to understand about this programme to know whether it is working and how to improve it?  

-   Make your Theory of Change visible and testable

    Your MEAL plan should map directly to your ToC not just reference it. Each key assumption should have a corresponding monitoring or evaluation mechanism. If an assumption cannot be tested, name why. Donors respect honesty about the limits of what can be known.  

-   Show how data will be used not just collected

    Most MEAL plans describe data collection in detail and say almost nothing about how findings will feed into decisions. Add a learning calendar: when will data be reviewed, by whom, and what kinds of decisions could it inform? This is what separates a compliance document from a genuine management tool.  

-   Be realistic about what you can measure with the resources available

    A MEAL plan with 47 indicators and a 3% budget line is not a plan it is a wish list. If your MEL budget cannot support your indicator list, say so and negotiate. Donors who see a realistic, well-costed MEAL plan trust it more than an ambitious one with no resources behind it.  

-   Build in adaptive management triggers

    Name, explicitly, the **conditions under which the programme would consider course-correcting**. What finding would prompt a programme review? What threshold of underperformance would trigger a design revision? This signals to donors that your MEAL plan is connected to how the programme actually operates.

# Shipping Quotes

For a ****quarter-container shipment from Porto to Limassol****, I would normally quote this as ****LCL (Less-than-Container Load / groupage)**** rather than trying to book 25% of a container yourself.  


<a id="org24338a6"></a>

## Quotation Details

20 FCL / 40 m³ (or under)  
Ask for a **door-to-door household relocation, approximately 40 m³, Porto → Limassol**, with the following explicitly included:  

-   Origin: Porto, Portugal
-   Destination: Limassol, Cyprus
-   Cargo: Personal household belongings / used furniture and personal effects
-   Estimated volume: 39 m³
-   Service required: Door-to-door
-   Preferred option: dedicated 20-ft container
-   Customs: Please include Cyprus customs clearance and advise on **Transfer of Residence** tax relief
-   Weekly port storage charges at destination
-   Please provide: Total door-to-door price, all origin/destination charges, estimated transit time and any exclusions.  
    
    I may need storage in Limassol for approximately 3 months before final delivery. Please quote **door-to-door with storage-in-transit**, including unloading the container into your warehouse/depot and final delivery to my address. Please separately identify all port storage/demurrage charges and the monthly storage rate.  
    
    On the quote, verify:

-   Loading
-   Local transport Porto → port
-   Optional weekly storage charges at port
-   Ocean/ferry transport to Limassol
-   Customs clearance in Cyprus
-   Optional weekly storage charges at port
-   Local transport from Limassol port to your address
-   Unloading
-   Any storage charges
-   All VAT, customs and other taxes clearly identified
-   Transit time
-   Validity of the quotation


### Private container storage around Limassol

At the port the charge is **EUR 18/day** after the first week.  

For example, **RTSCY** in the Limassol area currently advertises a 20-ft-sized storage unit for **€120/month + 19% VAT**, i.e. about **€143/month**. They describe it as temperature-regulated and give 24/7 access.  


### **Transfer of Residence** tax relief

Ask your Portuguese freight forwarder:  
"Please arrange the appropriate proof of Union status (T2L/T2LF) for my household goods shipment from Portugal to Cyprus."  
This is particularly worth doing for a large 40 m³ shipment.

## LCL vs. FCL shipping

"Quarter container" could mean very different things commercially. If you have roughly **5–8 m³**, LCL is likely appropriate. If you have **8–10+ m³**, it is worth getting \*\*both an LCL quote and a 20-foot FCL quote\*\*—the latter can sometimes become surprisingly competitive once LCL handling, consolidation, port charges and destination fees are included.  

When requesting quotes, give them:  

-   Collection address/postcode in Porto
-   Delivery address in Limassol
-   Number of pallets/crates
-   Dimensions of each
-   Total weight
-   Total volume in m³
-   Description of goods
-   Whether the goods are ****personal effects or commercial cargo****
-   Approximate value
-   Whether you need ****door-to-door****
-   Whether you need packing/unpacking
-   Desired shipping date
-   Whether you need customs clearance
